unit.title: Numbers Beyond 10 and Making Sense of Amounts

contentBlocks.text: Last week you put groups together. Today we do the opposite — taking some away and seeing how many are left!

Use 5 small objects (buttons, blocks, or crackers). Start with a group of 5, then take some away and count how many are left. For example: start with 5, take away 2 — count what's left: 1, 2, 3. There are 3 left! Try this with different starting amounts and different amounts taken away, always counting what remains.
You just practiced subtraction by physically taking objects away and counting what's left — real math you can touch and see! Tomorrow we'll look at breaking one number into two smaller parts.

objectives: Model subtraction within 5 by physically removing objects from a group and counting what remains
Solve simple take-away word problems within 5
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review putting groups together (addition) from last week.
2. Introduce taking away using 5 objects: start with 5, remove 2, count what's left.
3. Practice 2-3 more take-away examples together with real objects.
4. Move to the worksheet, using objects to solve each problem before writing the answer.
5. Close by explaining subtraction in one sentence: taking some away and counting what's left.
differentiationTips: Struggling: keep every problem starting from 5 or fewer, and always use real physical objects rather than working abstractly
Ready for more: ask the child to predict how many will be left before actually taking the objects away and counting
Physical, countable objects are essential here — this is a concrete precursor to abstract subtraction, not a symbolic exercise yet
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. 5 take away 2 leaves 3. 2. 4 take away 1 leaves 3. 3. 3 take away 1 leaves 2. 4. 5 take away 3 leaves 2. 5. 4 take away 2 leaves 2.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core standard K.OA.1/K.OA.2: representing and solving subtraction within 10 (scoped to within 5 here) using objects, drawings, or physical actions.
